claims.text: The studied material is an HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy.
The initial HfNbTaTiZr alloy is a single-phase BCC solid solution.
The constituent elements are randomly distributed in the initial alloy.
The constituent elements of HfNbTaTiZr have heterogeneous thermal expansion.
Differential thermal expansion among the elements generates localized thermal misfit stresses.
Thermal misfit stresses produce additional local lattice distortion and atomic-scale stress concentrations.
The resulting lattice distortions alter dislocation nucleation, mobility, and interactions.
Nanoscale coherent or evolving precipitates can interact with the proposed lattice distortions and dislocations.
Thermally induced lattice distortions enhance creep at high temperature.
Thermally induced lattice distortions increase dislocation pinning and strain hardening during cold deformation or aging.
Thermal misfit-induced lattice distortion modifies the alloy's elastic constants and thermoelastic response.
Relative to a mismatch-minimized baseline, standard HfNbTaTiZr will have a higher creep rate at approximately 1250 °C.
Relative to the baseline, standard HfNbTaTiZr will show more pronounced hardening after aging at 600–800 °C.
Standard HfNbTaTiZr will exhibit anomalous temperature dependence of its elastic moduli because thermal-misfit lattice distortions persist.
The thermal-mismatch effect is strongest near 1250 °C and during rapid thermal cycling.
A comparison between standard specimens and specimens processed by constraint or compositional modification can isolate thermal-expansion mismatch as the governing cause.
Creep, aging-related hardening, elastic moduli, and local lattice strain can be measured over the proposed temperature regimes.
Failure of mismatch minimization to change the mechanical responses, or failure to observe correlation between lattice distortion and those responses, would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: External mechanical constraint is presented as a way to minimize thermal-expansion mismatch, even though it does not remove constituent expansion differences and can itself create additional thermal stress. Compositional modification also changes the alloy chemistry, so it is not equivalent to constraining the same alloy.

Cold-work hardening and hardening after 600–800 °C aging are treated as the same response, although cold rolling and precipitation or aging hardening are distinct processing and strengthening phenomena.
